questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨4t+4,6t-21⟩\,,\,t>0.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨42,\,-18⟩$ when $t=4,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4t+4,6t-21⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (4t+4)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (6t-21)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}+4t+{C}_{1},\,3{t}^{2}-21t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨42,\,-18⟩.$ Substituting $t=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨2(4)^{2}+4(4)+{C}_{1},\,3(4)^{2}-21(4)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨42,\,-18⟩ & =⟨48+{C}_{1},\,-36+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=18.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨2{t}^{2}+4t-6,\,3{t}^{2}-21t+18⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2{t}^{2}+4t-6,\,3{t}^{2}-21t+18⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+4t-6=2(t-1)(t+3) & =0\,⇒\,t=-3,1, \\ 3{t}^{2}-21t+18=3(t-1)(t-6) & =0\,⇒\,t=1,6.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)⟩,\,0\le t<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t,\int (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =0\,⇒\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{3}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2} & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=\frac{\pi }{3},$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (t+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{3}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{3},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{2}^{3},\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{2}{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨1-3{t}^{2},4t-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,1⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1-3{t}^{2},4t-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (1-3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t,\int (4t-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t-{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},2{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨-1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨2-{2}^{3}+{C}_{1},2({2}^{2})-2+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,1⟩ & =⟨-6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=5$ and ${C}_{2}=-5.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t-{t}^{3}+5,2{t}^{2}-t-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1-{1}^{3}+5,2({1}^{2})-1-5⟩ \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t-3},2⟩,\,t>3.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,2⟩$ when $t=5,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t-3},2⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t-3}\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3)+{C}_{1},2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(5)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(5) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-3)+{C}_{1},2(5)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,2⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1},10+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3),2t-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3),2t-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=4, \\ 2t-8=2(t-4) & =0\,⇒\,t=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=4,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
